content.p: The Pagan's Motorcycle Club is among the best-known outlaw motorcycle gangs in the eastern United States. The US Department of Justice calls it a violent outlaw motorcycle gang whose members distribute cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, fentanyl and marijuana, and its members wear a diamond patch carrying the figure "1%". The Justice Department says the figure marks their claim to belong to the one percent of riders who do not obey the law.

Almost everything that can be checked about the club comes from prosecutors, indictments and sentencing. Over the past decade federal cases from Florida to Pittsburgh, North Carolina and Missouri have produced guilty verdicts, guilty pleas and prison terms for individual members, and indictments that are still only allegations. The club has not been dissolved by any of them.
content.h2: A 1959 beginning, and how little is firm
content.p: A motorcycle-gear retailer's history guide, Bobber Brothers, says an archived federal threat assessment from Virginia dates the Pagans to Prince George's County, Maryland, in 1959. According to that assessment the club began expanding in the 1960s by absorbing smaller clubs, and it was historically prominent in the Mid-Atlantic. The same guide notes that the assessment is old and describes a "mother club" as the central leadership at the time it was written. It also cautions that founder stories, early-member counts and other details found in secondary histories are not verified by the federal source, so it does not repeat them as fact.

The club's emblem is a seated, sword-bearing figure set against what looks like a sun. Secondary histories commonly say it is Surtr of Norse mythology, but the guide found no statement from the club explaining it and treats that reading as interpretation.

The guide also notes that the Pagans are commonly grouped with the Hells Angels, the Outlaws and the Bandidos as one of the "Big Four", and warns that this is historical shorthand and not a current ranking by size or danger.

The same guide points to one event from the club's violent history. An Associated Press account reported that authorities described a confrontation at the Hellraiser Ball in Plainview, New York, in 2002. Authorities told the AP that roughly 100 people identified as Pagans turned up, that a person identified as a Pagan died, that ten or more were hurt, and that 73 were charged. In 2011 a second AP report called one defendant one of 73 Pagans convicted in the case, after a plea in June 2002. The guide says it could not confirm the count against the federal docket and warns that a single incident does not show the intentions of every participant.

Federal prosecutors in Florida described the club's activity there after an investigation spanning a number of years. A January 2016 Justice Department release says the FBI infiltrated the club's Florida members and documented illegal distribution of drugs and guns. According to court records cited there, much of the conduct, including the firearms offences, took place at a former clubhouse in Sebastian, Florida. Other transactions happened in Miami, Fort Lauderdale, Fort Pierce, Stuart and Daytona Beach. Law enforcement bought 24 firearms from members and their associates, many of whom had prior convictions, and many of the weapons were stolen or had their serial numbers removed. Undercover officers also bought cocaine, prescription pills and marijuana.

The last two defendants were sentenced by US District Judge Donald L. Graham in Fort Pierce. Richard Todd Badali, 53, of Casselberry, whom the court was told was a ranking member in charge of all Pagans in Florida, was found guilty by a jury of selling a firearm to a convicted felon and possessing a firearm as a convicted felon. He received 18 months in prison. Thomas Richard Laakmann, 60, of Orange City, a rank-and-file member, was found guilty by a jury of selling a firearm to a convicted felon and of possessing a firearm after a domestic-violence misdemeanour conviction. He received 12 months. Both were barred from associating with club members while on supervised release.
Eight others who had pleaded guilty had already been sentenced. The terms ranged from probation for one man to 15 years for firearms offences in two cases, those of William Tendrich and Thomas Close.
content.h2: Pittsburgh: wiretaps and a clubhouse raid
content.p: In December 2020 a federal grand jury in Pittsburgh produced three related indictments naming 30 people from western Pennsylvania and eastern Ohio on drug-trafficking and gun charges. They were returned under seal on 1 December and made public a week later. The investigation began in August 2018 and, according to the Justice Department, led to court-authorised wiretaps on several telephones from August to November 2020.

The indictments allege conspiracies to distribute methamphetamine, cocaine and heroin during 2020. They target what prosecutors called the Pittsburgh chapter, including higher-ranking members, and a suspected member of an Ohio chapter. A separate firearms count accused a convicted felon of possessing a loaded pistol in October 2020. Agents executed search warrants at more than a dozen locations on 8 December 2020, among them the chapter's clubhouse at McKees Rocks. Prosecutors said the members routinely held "church", their weekly meeting, on Thursdays, and appeared to hold frequent large gatherings with non-members and with members of other outlaw clubs.

"For decades, the Pagans have used violence to control cocaine, heroin and meth trafficking throughout western Pennsylvania: that stops now," said US Attorney Scott W. Brady. The release states charges, not convictions.

The most severe sentence in the recent record came from North Carolina. Christopher Lamar Baker, 49, of Raleigh, was convicted in September of drug trafficking, firearm and money laundering charges after his arrest in November 2021. In early February 2023 US Attorney Michael Easley announced that Baker would serve 75 years in federal prison.

Prosecutors said Baker rose from chapter president in Raleigh to state leader and then national leader, and was one of "the 13", a group of national leaders who oversaw the purchase, trafficking and distribution of methamphetamine and illegal firearms. Over a 15-month investigation, agents found that he had supplied over 260 kilograms of methamphetamine to Raleigh and along the East Coast. Easley also said Baker had ordered a pledge's fingers cut off with a table saw as punishment for stealing from another member. He had also ordered the murder of a man who sold him fake drugs, according to officials from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. That man was placed in protective custody and was not hurt.

Baker was among 20 people arrested in Operation Diamond Ice, which an ATF agent described as a multi-organisation effort to disarm and dismantle outlaw motorcycle gangs. The Justice Department release spells it Operation Ice Diamond. Officials seized 46 firearms from members and affiliates, many of them illegal machine guns. At the news conference, the backdrop at the announcement included swastika motorcycle helmets, decorated axe handles for beatings and a wall hanging reading "Violence: The miracle cure for ignorance."

A week later another defendant from the same operation, Justin Matthew Fite, 31, a Kings Mountain-based member who pleaded guilty on 7 June 2022, was sentenced to 330 months in prison for armed drug trafficking. Police in Aiken County, South Carolina, had stopped his motorcycle in July 2021 and found nearly two kilograms of crystal methamphetamine in a saddlebag, which law enforcement said he was collecting for Baker. Fite was held accountable for distributing nearly five kilograms of methamphetamine between October 2020 and March 2022. The Justice Department described the club as a criminal enterprise with leaders across the United States and Puerto Rico.

Easley, the ATF's Bennie Mims and Raleigh's police chief could not say the organisation was defunct; lower-ranking members could potentially fill higher roles. Local coverage noted another killing: Jonas Barrett Padilla, 37, was shot and killed on his motorcycle in Raleigh on New Year's Day 2023. A roadside memorial carried the name "Lefty" and the letters "GFPD", described as a common Pagans moniker, and five members of the rival Red Devil gang were charged with his murder.
content.h2: Missouri and Kansas: the rival-club cases
content.p: In August 2024 federal prosecutors in Kansas City announced that 18 members and associates had been indicted for a series of armed assaults on members of rival clubs. The five-count indictment was returned under seal on 7 August 2024. An operation involving more than a dozen agencies produced 15 arrests and seven search warrants; two defendants were already in custody. Agents seized more than 40 firearms, thousands of rounds of ammunition, body armour and a marijuana grow.

The indictment says the Pagans maintain chapters in numerous states, including several active chapters in Missouri and Kansas. It alleges that the club is territorial and protects its area through violence and intimidation, that it threatened rivals found in areas it considered its own, and that it tried to eliminate other motorcycle gangs by assaulting, robbing, extorting and sometimes attempting to murder them. Its list of the club's primary Missouri rivals runs from the Hells Angels and the Outlaws to El Forastero, Galloping Goose, Sons of Silence and the Bandidos. Counts covered assaults alleged on 30 May 2022, 17 September 2022 and 20 July 2023, an attempted assault alleged on 3 September 2022, and the discharge of a firearm in the September assault.

One defendant's sentence was reported in November 2025. Brandon S. Hodge, 26, of Springfield, Missouri, was sentenced by US District Judge Greg Kays to 57 months in federal prison for assault with a dangerous weapon in aid of racketeering. Prosecutors said that on 17 September 2022 Hodge, then a prospect, and 12 other Pagans and members of a support club chased a lone rival from the road in Blue Springs, Missouri. Some of them carried firearms and at least one an axe handle. The man was shot seven times, with wounds to his knee, thigh, forearm, biceps, buttocks and the back of his leg. Prosecutors said several participants, Hodge among them, were afterwards awarded club patches for taking part.
content.h2: What the court record does and does not show
content.p: Guilty pleas, jury verdicts and prison terms bind only the named defendants and their conduct, and indictments remain allegations until proved. The cases do show the club's reach. Federal records place its members in Florida, Pennsylvania, Ohio, North Carolina, Missouri and Kansas, and the Justice Department says its leaders are spread across the United States and Puerto Rico. The Missouri indictment shows that the club has chapters well beyond the Mid-Atlantic.
No public source reviewed gives a reliable current membership count, a complete chapter list or a current organisational chart.
